title: The third sight: a dead man
hook: a funeral procession, the mourners weeping; the prince goes quiet

segments.voice: Yesterday: vyādhi, a man shaking with fever, and the prince learning sickness comes at any age. Your line: the body is borrowed. Today, the third ride.

Most of us remember a first funeral. The smell of the flowers. Shoes that pinched. An adult you'd never seen cry, crying. Something in the room could not be fixed. The prince had never had that day. Now Channa's chariot meets a crowd coming the other way, in mourning clothes, weeping, some beating their chests. On their shoulders, a bier. On the bier, a man wrapped in cloth, perfectly still. The prince watches them pass, and for a while says nothing.
screen: `YOUR FIRST FUNERAL.` → `A CROWD COMING THE OTHER WAY.` → `THE PRINCE GOES QUIET.`

segments.voice: When he asks, the question is simple. What is that? Channa says: a dead man. He won't see his mother or father again, and they won't see him. Will I die too? Yes. Everyone. Old age was slow. Sickness was sudden. Death is final. In the old stories he rides home shaken, and in some tellings cries out that it's shameful to be born, if this is where birth leads. The third sight adds something. It isn't only about my death. The mourners are the other half of the scene. Everyone we love will go, and we will go from them. That's why it hits hardest. A practice grows straight from this moment. The Buddha taught five things to reflect on often, and many monasteries chant them. I'm of the nature to grow old. I'm of the nature to become sick. I'm of the nature to die. Everything and everyone dear to me will change, and I'll be parted from them. My actions are the only thing I truly own. It can sound bleak. The teaching points the other way: not darker, vivid. The phone call you meant to make. The person across the kitchen table, who won't always be there. The Pali word for death is marana, and the Buddha's teaching is that looking at it calmly is how you stop wasting the time you have.
screen: `WHAT IS THAT?` · `THE MOURNERS ARE HALF THE SCENE.` · `FIVE THINGS TO REMEMBER.` · `NOT DARKER. VIVID.` · then, large: `EVERYONE WE LOVE WILL GO.`

segments.voice: Sit quietly, and bring to mind one person you have lost, recently or long ago, or someone still living whom you lost another way. Say their name, inside or out loud, and let a picture come: a laugh, a coat, the way they said your name. If tears or gratitude come, let them; nothing else is needed.
Marana. Death: a funeral on the road, and the prince learning it comes to everyone, and parts everyone from those they love.
Your line: everyone we love will go. Let it make you gentler, not afraid. Rest well.

screen: `DAY 33 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: THE FOURTH SIGHT: A WANDERER.`

howItsDone: In many Buddhist monasteries the five remembrances are chanted regularly, and Buddhists often reflect on death (maranasati) as a regular practice, sometimes at funerals where monks chant on impermanence.

fork.setup: you're the prince. a funeral procession passes, the mourners weeping. what do you do?
options: look away and tell Channa to drive faster.
fall quiet, and then ask what it is.
fork.reveal: he goes quiet, then asks. the answer, that everyone dies and is parted from those they love, sends him home shaken.

original.note: Pali and Sanskrit: death, dying. Maranasati is the practice of mindfulness of death.

trapdoor: what you thought: a sad story about a funeral.
what it means: the prince sees that death parts everyone from everyone they love, and the looking is what wakes him.
what a scholar hears: marana, from the root mṛ, to die; maranasati, mindfulness of death, and the five remembrances of AN 5.57 grow from this moment.

sources.ref: Mahapadana Sutta (Digha Nikaya 14): the dead man, the third sight, told of the earlier Buddha Vipassi
Nidanakatha (introduction to the Jataka): the prince's third sight on the road
Upajjhatthana Sutta (Anguttara Nikaya 5.57): five things to be reflected on often

notes: The five remembrances (AN 5.57) are paraphrased in the first person; they are not quoted from any translation. Confirm the paraphrase is faithful and appropriate to voice.
Channa's line that the dead man will not see his parents again follows DN 14's description of the dead; confirm.
'In some tellings he cries out that it's shameful to be born': DN 14 has Vipassi say 'shame on birth'. Confirm.
Etymology of marana from the root mr (to die); confirm.

Audit (second sample): the sources cited DN 14 alone for the prince's third sight, but DN 14 tells the four sights of the earlier Buddha Vipassi (with an unnamed charioteer); the prince-and-Channa telling is from later biographies. The DN 14 source now says so and the Nidanakatha is added. Days 32 and 34 have the same citation pattern (not edited in this audit).

Repair (job 2): for consistency, the teach no longer says monasteries chant them 'each morning' or that people who say them 'every day' 'often report the opposite' (no source given); howItsDone and the match game now say 'chanted regularly' / 'chanted in many monasteries'.
